title: Portfolio & Self-Assessment

pts: A portfolio collects a learner's work over time, selected to demonstrate development and range, not just final polish.
The European Language Portfolio framework popularised this approach specifically for language learning contexts.
This directly extends the can-do-based placement approach from Unit 2's needs analysis into ongoing assessment.
points.who: The Council of Europe's European Language Portfolio

v: A folder per learner; a one-page passport template

items: Show a sample portfolio folder and explain its three parts: passport, biography, work collection.
Learners complete a language passport: every language they use, where, with whom, and how well.
Learners rate their English on four skills using simple can-do statements.
Learners decorate the folder cover and write their name in all their languages.
Collect folders and store them in class, labelled by bench or roll number.
Learners interview a family member about the languages they use and add a short note.
Support: the passport template with pictures and home-language headings.
Challenge: a short paragraph on ‘My languages and me’.

blocks.x: A passport entry (written for this book):

lines: Name: Shabana. Languages: Urdu (home, with family, very well); Kannada (school and friends, well); English (school, TV, a little every day); Hindi (films, understanding well, speaking a little).
English, speaking: I can introduce myself and talk about my family.

blocks.x: The passport makes every language visible. Learners who feel weak in English often discover they are already skilled users of two or three languages.

body: Purpose: to show the structure of a language portfolio. Content: an open folder with three labelled sections: a passport with small language flags drawn as speech bubbles in different scripts, a biography with a notebook and a goal list, and a dossier with drafts and finished pieces. Style: warm, handmade. Board version: a folder with three pockets.

items: Google Docs (free) passport template for learners with access.

blocks.x: A card folder or a large envelope per learner.

pts: Include a mix of drafts and finished pieces, showing revision and development, not only best final versions.
Involve learners in selecting what goes in — the selection process itself builds valuable self-assessment skill.
Include work across skills and genres, connecting to Unit 33's genre range and Unit 3's four-skills integration.

items: Learners keep all English work for four weeks in a ‘working folder’.
At the end of the period, they choose three pieces for the portfolio: one they are proud of, one that shows improvement (with its first draft), and one that was difficult.
Each learner writes a one-line reason for each choice.
Pairs explain their choices to each other.
Remaining work goes home or is recycled.
Include one piece of speaking evidence: a recorded voice note, or a teacher’s observation slip.
Support: sentence frames for reasons.
Challenge: choose pieces from different skills and genres (Unit 33).

lines: I chose this because I used paragraphs for the first time.
I chose this draft and final version because you can see I corrected my past tenses.
I chose this because it was hard. I did not understand the listening at first.

blocks.x: Selection is itself a self-assessment skill: to choose a piece that shows improvement, a learner must know what improvement looks like.

body: Purpose: to show selection. Content: a thick, messy working folder on the left; an arrow labelled ‘choose three’; a slim portfolio on the right with three pieces, each tagged ‘proud’, ‘improved’, ‘difficult’. Style: clear, cheerful. Board version: two rectangles and an arrow.

items: Google Drive (free) folders, one per learner, for digital work.

pts: CEFR can-do checklists, introduced for placement in Unit 2, work equally well for ongoing self-assessment across a course.
Learners checking their own progress against concrete can-do statements builds the metacognition adult learners bring (Unit 16).
Regular, brief self-assessment check-ins normalise reflection as a routine part of the course, not a special event.

v: A can-do checklist for the current unit

items: At the start of a unit, give learners a checklist of five can-do statements linked to the unit aims.
Learners mark each: ‘not yet’, ‘with help’, ‘on my own’.
Every two weeks, learners review and update their marks, adding one piece of evidence for any change.
The teacher scans a sample of checklists to spot patterns.
At the end of the unit, learners set one goal for the next.
Use a traffic-light version for younger learners: red, amber, green.
Support: statements with pictures and home-language glosses.
Challenge: learners write one can-do statement of their own.

blocks.x: A checklist for a B1 unit on travel (written for this book, based on the CEFR style of descriptor):

lines: I can ask for and understand directions in a town.
I can buy a ticket and ask about times.
I can write a short message to a friend about a trip.
I can understand the main points of a travel announcement.
I can describe a place I have visited.

blocks.x: This extends the placement checklist from Unit 2 into ongoing assessment, and builds the kind of metacognition described in Unit 16.

body: Figure 42.3 Not yet, with help, on my own

Purpose: to show self-assessment over time. Content: a checklist with five statements and three columns; small ticks move from ‘not yet’ to ‘on my own’ across three dated check-ins, drawn in different colours. Style: clean, tabular. Board version: a three-column grid.

items: Google Forms (free) with a multiple-choice grid for each check-in.

blocks.x: A printed checklist glued inside the portfolio cover.

pts: Brief reflective notes accompanying each piece — what was hard, what improved — turn a folder of work into a genuine learning record.
This connects to Unit 9's reflective-practice principle, applied to the learner's own development rather than the teacher's.
Scaffold reflective writing with prompts initially; unscaffolded reflection is a skill that develops over time.

items: Model a reflection on your own learning, for example learning a few words of a new language.
Give learners a slip with three prompts (see model language).
Learners attach a completed slip to each portfolio piece.
Read a sample of slips and respond briefly to one or two.
Over the term, reduce the prompts until learners write freely.
Learners may write reflections in the home language at first, with key words in English.
Support: sentence starters and a word bank (easier, harder, improved, still need).
Challenge: compare this piece with an earlier one.

lines: What was hard about this task?
What did I do better this time?
What will I try next time?
The hard part was the ending. This time I used ‘first, then, finally’. Next time I will check my spelling before I give it.

blocks.x: Reflection turns a folder of work into a learning record. It applies the reflective-practice principle from Unit 9 to the learner.

body: Purpose: to show reflection attached to work. Content: a handwritten paragraph with a small coloured slip stapled to its corner, showing the three prompts and brief answers. Style: realistic, close-up. Board version: a rectangle with a smaller rectangle at its corner.

items: Padlet (free plan) for short reflections alongside photographed work.

blocks.x: Pre-cut coloured slips kept in a box on the teacher’s table.

body: Reflection is a skill that develops slowly. Early reflections will be short and general (It was good). Respond to them with one specific question (What exactly was better?) rather than a grade.

pts: Assess range, development over time, and quality of reflection, not only the polish of the single best piece included.
This distributes assessment weight across a course's full arc, rather than concentrating it in one high-stakes moment.
Share assessment criteria with learners from the start, so portfolio-building is purposeful throughout, not retrospective.

v: 3–5 minutes per learner, across two weeks

items: Share the criteria at the start of term: range, development, reflection, and quality of the best piece.
Near the end of term, meet each learner briefly while the class works on a task.
The learner explains two pieces and their reflections.
Agree a mark against the criteria, and one goal.
Record the result in the register or a simple sheet.
In very large classes, meet groups of four, each learner presenting one piece.
Support: the learner may explain in the home language, then say one sentence in English.
Challenge: the learner proposes their own mark with reasons.

lines: Range: work from at least three skills and two genres.
Development: clear evidence of improvement between drafts or over time.
Reflection: specific comments on what was learned.
Quality: the best piece meets the unit’s success criteria.
T: Which piece shows your biggest improvement?
S1: This letter. In the first draft there were no paragraphs. Now there are three.

blocks.x: Hamp-Lyons and Condon (2000) stress that portfolio assessment needs clear, shared criteria if it is to be fair.

body: Purpose: to show multi-dimensional assessment. Content: a wheel divided into four segments labelled ‘Range’, ‘Development’, ‘Reflection’, ‘Quality’, each shaded to a different level for one learner. Style: clean, colourful. Board version: a circle in four parts.

items: Google Sheets (free) to record criteria scores.

blocks.x: A criteria sheet in each portfolio, completed during the conference.

pts: Digital portfolio tools make ongoing collection, organisation and teacher access considerably more manageable than paper folders.
This connects to Unit 18's digital-tools principles — the tool should serve the portfolio's purpose, not complicate it.
Ensure access equity (Unit 18's digital divide) is considered before requiring a fully digital-only system.

items: Survey learners: who has regular access to a phone, a computer or the internet, and when?
List what a digital portfolio would make easier: storage, audio, sharing with parents.
List who would be excluded if the system were digital only.
Design a mixed system: paper as the default, digital as an option.
Review after one term.
Parents or older siblings photograph paper work and share it on a class WhatsApp group, with consent.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Everyone keeps a paper folder in class. Learners with a phone may add voice recordings via the class Google Classroom. The teacher photographs one speaking sample per term for learners without phones.

blocks.x: Unit 18 raised the digital divide. A portfolio that relies on devices some learners lack measures access, not language.

body: Purpose: to show an equitable mixed system. Content: two paths, one with a paper folder and one with a phone, leading to the same portfolio at the end. Style: clean, inclusive. Board version: two arrows meeting.

items: Google Classroom (free for schools) to collect digital work.
Seesaw (free basic version; paid features) for younger learners’ portfolios. [VERIFY current free-tier features]

blocks.x: Paper folders stored in a class cupboard, with the teacher’s phone used for a few audio samples.

pts: A visible, growing body of work builds a tangible sense of progress that a single test score rarely conveys as clearly.
This connects to Unit 22's self-efficacy research — visible evidence of growth reliably supports persistence.
This is especially valuable at the intermediate levels, where progress can otherwise feel slow or invisible.

v: 15 minutes at the end of each term
Portfolios; a wall space or chart paper

items: Learners place their first piece of the year next to their most recent one.
They write one sentence on a sticky note: Then I…, now I….
Volunteers add their notes to a class progress wall.
Read a few aloud; ask the class what kinds of progress they notice.
Keep the wall up for a few weeks as a reminder.
A ‘then and now’ exhibition for parents on open day.
Support: the sentence frame on the board.
Challenge: describe progress in two skills.

lines: In June I wrote four sentences. Now I write two paragraphs.
In June I did not understand the listening. Now I understand the main idea.

blocks.x: At B1–B2, progress can feel slow and invisible. A visible body of work provides the kind of success evidence that supports self-efficacy (Bandura 1997; Unit 22).

body: Purpose: to show progress made visible. Content: two sheets of work side by side, a short uneven paragraph labelled ‘June’ and a longer, organized one labelled ‘November’, with a sticky note between them reading Then I…, now I…. Style: warm, realistic. Board version: two rectangles of different sizes.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers) to design a class progress display.

blocks.x: Chart paper and sticky notes, or paper slips and glue.

pts: Portfolios work well alongside, not necessarily instead of, the formal testing principles from Unit 21.
Use portfolios for development-over-time evidence and formal tests for standardised, comparable snapshots where those are genuinely needed.
The combination gives a fuller assessment picture than either method delivers alone.

items: List the formal assessments you must give this term (unit tests, term exams).
List what they measure well, and what they miss.
Decide what the portfolio will add: development, speaking, writing process, reflection.
Decide the weight of each element, within school rules.
Explain the plan to learners and parents.
Plan jointly with other English teachers of the same grade for consistency.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Term exam: reading, grammar, controlled writing (standardized, comparable).
Portfolio: two writing pieces with drafts, one speaking sample, can-do checklists, reflections (development over time).
Teacher observation: participation in pair and group tasks.

blocks.x: The combination gives a fuller picture than either alone. Formal tests (Unit 21) offer comparability; portfolios offer evidence of growth.

body: Purpose: to show the complementary roles of tests and portfolios. Content: a single photograph labelled ‘Test: a snapshot’ next to an open photo album labelled ‘Portfolio: a story over time’, both placed on the same desk under a heading ‘The full picture’. Style: gentle, symbolic. Board version: a rectangle and a book.

items: Google Sheets (free) for an assessment plan grid.

blocks.x: A one-page plan in the teacher’s record book.

body: Start small. With one class, run only ‘Choose three’ and the reflection slip for one term. At the end, hold a two-minute conference with ten learners. Decide from that experience what to add next term.

dek: Unit 42 of 100: tracking real development across a course through a growing, learner-curated body of work — a fuller picture than any single test can offer.

aims.x: Unit 21 introduced portfolios as one alternative to formal testing. This unit builds the actual system: what a language portfolio is, what goes into it, how learners assess and reflect on their own work, how the teacher assesses the whole, and how a portfolio can run in a class of fifty with few devices.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: explain the purpose and structure of a language portfolio;
guide learners in selecting evidence that shows development;
use can-do checklists for regular self-assessment;
scaffold short reflective writing about learners’ own work;
assess a portfolio for range, development and reflection;
choose between paper, digital and mixed portfolio systems fairly;
use portfolios to make progress visible and support motivation;
combine portfolio evidence with formal tests in a single assessment plan.

why: Why this matters. Unit 21 introduced portfolios as an alternative to formal testing. This poster builds the actual system: what goes in, how it's assessed, and how learners self-reflect on it.

background.x: A test gives a snapshot; a portfolio gives an album. The idea is simple: learners collect work over time, choose pieces that show what they can do and how they have developed, and comment on them. In language education the best-known model is the European Language Portfolio (ELP), developed by the Council of Europe alongside the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (Council of Europe 2001). The ELP has three parts: a language passport summarizing a learner’s languages and levels, a language biography in which learners set goals and reflect on their learning, and a dossier of selected work. David Little (2005) argues that its central value lies in involving learners in assessing themselves against can-do descriptors, which develops their capacity to take charge of their own learning.

Self-assessment has long attracted scepticism: will learners not simply overrate themselves? Research suggests that accuracy improves when descriptors are concrete and learners have practice and feedback (Oscarson 1989). More importantly, the purpose of self-assessment in a portfolio is formative. Black and Wiliam’s (1998) influential review showed that formative assessment, including learners’ involvement in judging their own work, can raise achievement. Zimmerman (2002) describes self-monitoring and self-evaluation as core processes in self-regulated learning.

India already has a strong policy basis for this kind of assessment. Continuous and comprehensive evaluation was introduced under the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act 2009, and the NEP 2020 calls for a holistic, ‘360-degree’ progress card that includes self-assessment and peer assessment alongside teacher assessment (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020: para. 4.35 [VERIFY paragraph number]). The NCF 2023 likewise encourages portfolios as a record of learning (NCERT 2023). A language portfolio can welcome a learner’s multilingual repertoire too: the ELP’s language passport records all the learner’s languages, not only the one being studied, which fits naturally with NEP’s view of home languages as a resource.

items: Portfolio criteria. Assess range, development, reflection and quality with shared criteria.
Self-assessment accuracy. Compare learners’ can-do ratings with your observations and discuss differences.
Reflection quality. Track how specific learners’ reflections become over a term.
Learner voice. Ask: ‘Did the portfolio help you see your progress? How?’
What evidence of development do your current assessments capture, and what do they miss?
Who chooses the work that represents your learners: you or them?
How accurate are your learners’ self-assessments, and how could you help them improve?
Could a portfolio work in your class without devices?
How might you make learners’ other languages visible in their portfolios?
What would you need to explain to parents about portfolio assessment?

terms.def: A description of what a learner can do in a language, as in the CEFR, used for setting goals, self-assessment and describing levels; for example, ‘I can write a short email inviting a friend.’

The part of a language portfolio in which learners keep selected samples of their work, such as drafts, finished pieces and recordings, as evidence of what they can do in the language (Council of Europe 2001).
A Council of Europe document in which learners record and reflect on their language learning, with three parts: a language passport, a language biography and a dossier (Council of Europe 2001).
Assessment used during learning to guide the next steps in teaching and learning, through questioning, observation, feedback and self- and peer assessment (Black and Wiliam 1998).
The part of a language portfolio in which learners describe their language learning experiences, set goals and reflect on their progress (Council of Europe 2001).
The part of a language portfolio that summarizes a learner’s languages, self-assessed levels, certificates and intercultural experiences (Council of Europe 2001).
A purposeful collection of a learner’s work over time, often with reflections, which shows progress and supports assessment for learning.

The process of thinking back on one’s learning or teaching in order to understand it and decide what to do next. For learners, it may take the form of a short reflection slip attached to a piece of portfolio work.

Learners judging their own performance or progress against criteria, for example with ‘can do’ statements or a checklist. It builds awareness, responsibility and autonomy, and gives the teacher useful information.

Learning in which learners plan, monitor and evaluate their own learning, managing goals, strategies, motivation and time (Zimmerman 2000). Also called self-regulation, it is developed through goal-setting, self-monitoring and reflection.
